passage:
"So who's leading?" Anjali asked, stirring her coffee in the canteen.
"Joseph, obviously," said Rafiq. "Did you hear his pitch in class? Like a real CEO."
"Exactly," Anjali said. "He talks like someone who runs companies."
Kiran looked up from her laptop. "Last semester, Joseph's group submitted two days late."
"That was probably the group's fault."
"And Hemlata did all their data work. On time."
"Hemlata barely speaks in meetings," Anjali said. "Leaders need to speak."
"Leaders need to deliver," Kiran said quietly.
Joseph arrived, grinning, and announced a "bold vision". Anjali nodded along. Two weeks later the draft was missing, Joseph was "still ideating", and Hemlata stayed up finishing it alone.

qa.q: Who did all the data work for Joseph's group last semester?
qa.a: Hemlata did all their data work, on time.

qa.q: Why does Anjali feel Joseph is the obvious leader?
qa.a: His confident, polished way of talking matches her picture of someone who runs things, so it feels like proof of ability even though his record says otherwise.

qa.q: What went wrong in choosing the leader, and what could fix it?
qa.a: They picked the best talker instead of checking who had delivered before; next time the group could look at past work and deadlines, which would point to Hemlata.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemlata to finish the draft alone?
qa.a: Hemlata carries the real work while the title went to someone else, which is likely tiring and feels unfair.

grounding: Shows a student assuming the fluent, confident speaker will run the project well while overlooking the quieter teammate who delivers.

passage: Last year I chose the wrong head for our college fest committee, and I still think about why. I'm Chandrika, the one who ran the vote. Amandeep gave a speech that made the whole room clap: big sponsors, a famous DJ, "the best fest this city has seen." Sonam, who had quietly handled permissions and budgets for two years, said only, "I'll make sure it runs on time." I remember thinking Sonam sounded small. Amandeep sounded like a leader. So I pushed the committee his way. Three weeks before the fest, no sponsor had signed and the stage booking had lapsed. Sonam fixed most of it in ten days. I'd mistaken a good speech for a good plan.

qa.q: What did Sonam say during the speeches?
qa.a: Sonam said only, "I'll make sure it runs on time."

qa.q: Why did Chandrika push the committee toward Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep's speech drew claps and sounded like a leader, while Sonam's plain line sounded small, so style felt like proof of competence.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do differently when choosing a head next time?
qa.a: Chandrika could ask each candidate about past work, like permissions and budgets handled, and weigh that record above how impressive a speech sounds.

qa.q: How might Sonam have felt stepping in three weeks before the fest?
qa.a: Sonam may have felt frustrated at being passed over but responsible toward the fest, which is why the fixing still got done.

grounding: Shows a student backing the confident speaker as fest head and overlooking the quieter, more reliable teammate.

passage:
Faculty mentor's note, semester project review. Prof. Pallavi Rao.
Observation: When the second-year design group chose its project lead, Himani argued strongly for Devraj, who presents fluently and confidently. She described Farzana, who speaks little, as "not leadership material." Yet Farzana's lab logs were the only complete ones in the group, and her prototype was the one that worked in the demo. Under Devraj, two deadlines slipped. When I asked Himani what she had based her choice on, she said, "He just seemed like he'd know what to do."
Action taken: I asked the group to review each member's actual contributions from the logs, and suggested they rotate the lead for the next phase. Himani agreed to propose Farzana.

qa.q: Whose lab logs were the only complete ones?
qa.a: Farzana's lab logs were the only complete ones in the group.

qa.q: What does Himani's answer, "He just seemed like he'd know what to do," reveal about her thinking?
qa.a: It shows she judged by how confident and fluent Devraj sounded, not by any record, so his style felt like competence to her.

qa.q: How did Prof. Pallavi Rao help the group correct the choice?
qa.a: The mentor asked them to review each member's real contributions in the logs and to rotate the lead, which puts evidence above impressions.

qa.q: How might Farzana see being called "not leadership material"?
qa.a: Farzana may feel overlooked and discouraged, since her complete logs and working prototype were not counted as leadership.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a fluent, confident teammate as lead and overlooking the quieter one whose work was more reliable.

passage:
Saturday, 2 a.m., hackathon, day 2
I picked the wrong team lead and I know it now.
Yesterday at the kickoff, Pankaj gave this amazing pitch: hands moving, jokes, words like "scalable" and "user journey." Everyone clapped. I thought, obviously he's leading, he sounds like someone who runs a startup. Salma, who sits next to me in the lab, said almost nothing. She just asked two quiet questions about the database. I didn't even think of her.
Now it's 2 a.m. Pankaj has been "networking" at the snack table for three hours. Salma has built the whole backend, fixed my login bug, and quietly written a task list on the whiteboard that everyone is following.
I think I confused sounding good with being good. I'm Hrithik, 20, supposedly smart, and I fell for a speech.
Tomorrow I'll suggest Salma presents the demo too.

qa.q: What has Salma built by 2 a.m.?
qa.a: She has built the whole backend.

qa.q: Why did it feel obvious to Hrithik that Pankaj should lead?
qa.a: Pankaj's confident pitch, with jokes and startup words, matched Hrithik's picture of a leader, so the style felt like proof of skill.

qa.q: What choice does Hrithik make for tomorrow, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Hrithik will suggest Salma presents the demo too, giving credit and visibility to the teammate whose work is actually holding the project together.

qa.q: How might Salma feel if she is asked to present the demo?
qa.a: She may be nervous about speaking up but pleased that her quiet, steady work has finally been noticed.

grounding: A student at a hackathon realises the team lead was chosen for a fluent, confident pitch while a quiet, more reliable teammate was overlooked.

passage:
12 October, hostel room, late
Survey deadline today. Guess who delivered? Not Manoj.
Three weeks ago I voted for him as group leader without thinking twice. He gave that speech in the first class without notes, sounded like someone on a TV panel, used words like "synergy" and made everyone laugh. Bindu didn't even raise her hand. She just sat there with her colour-coded planner.
Today Manoj had "a few directions we could explore" and no survey. Bindu had quietly made the whole questionnaire, tested it on her roommates and uploaded it at 6 a.m. Nobody asked her to.
I voted in about three seconds, just from how he talks. I still like listening to him. I just don't think I'd trust him with a deadline again.
Rekha

qa.q: What time did Bindu upload the questionnaire?
qa.a: At 6 a.m.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling about the vote now?
qa.a: Rekha feels frustrated and a bit foolish for voting in three seconds because of Manoj's smooth speech, while still enjoying listening to him.

qa.q: What could the group look at next time it picks a leader?
qa.a: Who plans the work and meets small deadlines, like Bindu with her planner and tested questionnaire, rather than who gives the best speech.

qa.q: How might Bindu feel doing the work without being chosen?
qa.a: Bindu might feel unnoticed or taken for granted, since she did the survey unasked while Manoj got the title.

grounding: A student's diary shows choosing a fluent, confident speaker as leader and overlooking a quieter, more reliable teammate.

passage: The NSS camp in a village near Kolar had one job for the week: map every household's water source. Maria, the group coordinator, needed a team lead. Ramesh stood up in the panchayat hall and spoke to the sarpanch like a politician, full of big words about development. "He's our man," Maria wrote in her notebook on the spot. Pallavi, who had quietly asked for a village map on the first day, was given the job of carrying water bottles. By Wednesday Ramesh had given two more speeches and visited nine houses. Pallavi, on her own evening walks, had marked all eighty-four wells and taps on the map in blue ink. When the professor asked for the survey, it was Pallavi's map that Maria handed over, red-faced.

qa.q: How many wells and taps did Pallavi mark?
qa.a: Eighty-four, in blue ink.

qa.q: Why was Maria red-faced handing over Pallavi's map?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed, because she had picked Ramesh for his confident speeches and given Pallavi, who did the real work, the water bottles.

qa.q: What went wrong in choosing the lead, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: Maria chose by speaking style; next time she could give a small task first and see who plans and finishes it, as Pallavi did with the map.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about being handed the water bottles?
qa.a: Pallavi may have felt overlooked and a little hurt, yet she kept going and quietly finished the survey anyway.

grounding: A student coordinator picks a confident speaker as lead and overlooks a quiet teammate who actually completes the survey.

Dear Anirban,

Remember the robotics project last term, when I chose Kunal as team lead over you? I owe you a letter.

Kunal talked like a CEO. He had the jargon, the posture, the "let's crush this" energy. You barely spoke in meetings, just nodded and took notes. I thought: Kunal will make us win.

Then Kunal missed two deadlines, and you stayed up three nights fixing the motor code he had promised to write. At the competition, it was your code that worked. I didn't even say thank you properly.

I think I mistook confidence for competence. It's embarrassing to admit. You were the reliable one all along, and I didn't see it because you were quiet.

Next project, I'd like you to lead, if you're willing.

Amandeep

qa.q: What is Amandeep doing to fix the mistake?
qa.a: Amandeep admits the error, thanks Anirban and asks Anirban to lead next time, based on what Anirban actually did.

passage:
You want to hear about the hackathon? Okay, Ramesh, this one's partly about you, so don't laugh.

I'm Mehak. Second year, we had forty-eight hours to build an app for a college fest. I had to pick a team lead. There was Vikram, who spoke like a conference speaker. Smooth, confident, full of big words. And there was Ramesh, who barely spoke in the first meeting but had already sketched the database on a napkin.

I picked Vikram. Obviously. He looked like a leader.

By hour thirty, Vikram had redesigned the logo four times and given two motivational speeches. The code was a mess. Ramesh quietly stayed up all night fixing the backend. We submitted with twelve minutes left, only because of him.

We didn't win. But I learned something. I had mistaken the way Vikram talked for the way he worked. The quiet one was the one I could trust.

qa.a: We had forty-eight hours.

qa.q: Why did Mehak pick Vikram as lead?
qa.a: Mehak felt confident in Vikram because he was smooth and fluent, and that style felt like proof he would lead well.

qa.q: What could Mehak do the next time Mehak picks a team lead?
qa.a: Mehak could look at what each person has actually done, like Ramesh's napkin sketch, rather than how they speak.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when Vikram was picked over him?
qa.a: Ramesh may have felt overlooked and a bit hurt, but he stayed and did the work anyway.

passage:
Monday, first week of term. Ritu had to choose a project partner for the business case competition. Eshaan gave a dazzling five-minute talk in class about start-ups, full of phrases like "disruption" and "scalable vision". Ritu signed up with him on the spot. A quiet classmate, Noor, who had topped last year's accounts paper, asked to join. Ritu said the team was full.

Thursday, two weeks later. Eshaan hadn't sent a single slide. He was "still thinking about the big picture". Ritu stayed up till two doing the numbers herself.

Monday, competition day. Eshaan's opening was brilliant. Then the judges asked about the cost figures. He stammered and looked at Ritu. She answered, but the team came fifth.

Noor's team won. Her numbers were flawless.

On the walk home, Ritu admitted to herself that she'd chosen Eshaan for how he sounded, not for anything he had ever done.

qa.q: What paper had Noor topped last year?
qa.a: Last year's accounts paper.

qa.q: What did Ritu feel and admit to herself on the walk home?
qa.a: Ritu felt disappointed and regretful, admitting she had chosen Eshaan for how he sounded, not for anything he had done.

qa.q: How could Ritu choose a partner more wisely next time?
qa.a: Ritu could look at people's past work and ask what they will actually contribute before deciding, instead of judging by a talk.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt when Ritu said the team was full?
qa.a: Noor may have felt brushed aside and a bit hurt, and perhaps quietly satisfied when her own team won.

grounding: A student chooses a fluent speaker as project partner over a quieter, stronger classmate, and sees it go wrong over weeks.

passage:
Siddharth, you're choosing your group leader because he "sounds like a boss"? Come, let me tell you something from my college days. I'm Elizabeth, and yes, I made the same mistake.

Final year, we had to run the department's cultural festival. There was Rohan, who spoke beautifully, always had a joke and a plan, and wore a blazer to meetings. And there was Meenakshi, who said very little but had run the canteen accounts for two years without a mistake.

I voted for Rohan. Most of us did.

By festival week, nothing was booked. The sound system didn't arrive. Rohan gave a speech about "vision" to a hall with no microphone.

Meenakshi quietly phoned vendors all night and saved the fest.

That taught me that a smooth voice and a blazer aren't the same as someone who shows up.

So, before you vote, beta, who in your group actually finishes things?

qa.q: How long had Meenakshi run the canteen accounts?
qa.a: For two years without a mistake.

qa.q: What was young Elizabeth likely feeling when she voted for Rohan?
qa.a: Young Elizabeth felt impressed and confident in Rohan, because his speech, jokes and blazer looked like leadership.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Elizabeth's story, and what does it show?
qa.a: When Rohan gave a speech to a hall with no microphone while Meenakshi saved the fest overnight, it showed that style isn't the same as reliability.

qa.q: How might Meenakshi have felt during festival week?
qa.a: Meenakshi may have felt frustrated at being overlooked but determined to save the fest anyway.

grounding: An elder recalls choosing a fluent, confident leader over a quieter, reliable classmate, and what it cost.

passage:
The college tech fest was during Diwali week, and the student team had only ten days to build their app demo. Arohi had to choose a project lead between two teammates.
Rishabh spoke beautifully. In the first meeting he talked about "vision" and "disrupting campus life" with his hands moving, and everyone nodded. Shankar barely spoke. He sat at the back with a notebook and asked one question: "Who's testing the login?"
Arohi picked Rishabh. He sounded like a leader.
By day six, the demo didn't work. Rishabh had made three more slide decks and no code plan. Shankar, meanwhile, had quietly fixed the login, written a testing checklist and messaged everyone their tasks.
On day nine, with the power going off in the hostel, it was Shankar who organised a laptop rotation so the build finished on time.
Arohi watched him at two in the morning, calm, ticking off the checklist, and felt her stomach drop. She had mistaken the voice for the work.

qa.q: Who organised the laptop rotation on day nine?
qa.a: Shankar organised the laptop rotation.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel watching Shankar at two in the morning?
qa.a: She felt a sinking regret, realising she had chosen Rishabh for his confident speaking rather than for reliable work.

qa.q: What could Arohi do differently when choosing a lead next time?
qa.a: She could look at what each person has actually done, like past projects or task plans, rather than how fluently they speak in meetings.

qa.a: Shankar might feel tired and a little overlooked, though also proud that the demo finished on time.
